title: Expand Option Groups Into Words
statement:
A pattern s describes a set of words. Outside braces, every letter is fixed. A group in braces like {x,y,z} means "exactly one of these letters goes here". Groups are never nested, and the letters inside one group are distinct.

Return every word the pattern can produce, sorted in alphabetical order.

examples.why: 2 × 2 = 4 words. The second group is written c before b, yet the output must still be sorted.
No groups: the pattern is exactly one word.
A group with a single letter acts like a fixed letter.

constraints: s has lowercase letters, commas and braces only
Braces are balanced and never nested; each group has at least one letter, separated by single commas
hints: First turn the pattern into a list of slots, where each slot is a list of allowed letters. A fixed letter is a slot with one option.
Now build words one slot at a time: for each option in the current slot, append it and move on to the next slot. When you run out of slots, you have a full word.
Sort each slot's options before you start. Then the depth-first order produces the words already in alphabetical order, with no final sort.

explain.intuition:
The pattern is a sequence of slots. Each slot is either one fixed letter or a group of choices. The words are every way to pick one option per slot, which is a cartesian product, and backtracking enumerates it: choose an option for slot 0, recurse into slot 1, and so on, undoing the choice on the way back.

Ordering comes for free. If every slot's options are sorted, a depth-first walk that tries options left to right emits words in dictionary order, for the same reason that counting with digits emits numbers in order. All words have the same length, so no shorter-prefix cases can break it.
steps: Parse s into slots: on {, read letters up to } skipping commas, and sort them; otherwise a single letter is its own slot.
Run dfs(i, word): if i equals the number of slots, record word.
Otherwise, for each option c in slot i, call dfs(i + 1, word + c).
Return the recorded words; they are already sorted.
pitfalls: Forgetting to sort. The options inside a group can be listed in any order, as in {c,b}.
Treating the commas as letters, or splitting the whole string on commas, which breaks the fixed letters around the groups.
Moving the index to the closing brace but not past it, so the } is then read as a fixed letter.

complexity.time: O(W · L), where W is the number of words and L their length

solutions.title: Build the product slot by slot, then sort
solutions.idea: Start with [""] and, for each slot, extend every partial word with every option. Sort at the end.

solutions.title: Backtracking over sorted slots
solutions.idea: Parse into slots with sorted options; a depth-first walk then produces words in alphabetical order.

followups: Groups may now nest and contain whole words, like "{a,{bc,d}}e". How does the parser change, and how do you remove duplicates?
Return only the k-th word in sorted order without generating all of them.
